title: Neoclouds: These firms you've never heard of are feeding fears the AI bubble could burst
description: Neocloud firms often finance themselves by signing long-term lease contracts with major tech customers who need quick access to computing power.Firms
body: Neocloud firms often finance themselves by signing long-term lease contracts with major tech customers who need quick access to computing power.Firms can then borrow money using those contracts – plus the AI chips they purchase – as collateral, explained analyst Cory Johnson of "The Quiet Period" IPO research outfit.He said debt is common across neocloud firms because the hardware has to be paid for up front.Take the industry leader: CoreWeave. It's a fraction of the size of some of the Big Tech companies it serves.But Johnson believes lenders sometimes consider the creditworthiness of CoreWeave's customers, like Microsoft or Meta, more than the company's when they lend."This helps explain how CoreWeave accumulated $35.1bn (£26.3bn) in debt," he said.Some jittery investors appear to be having second thoughts.CoreWeave stock has lost a quarter of its value over the past month, and it's not alone.Shares in other neocloud firms like Nebius, IREN, and Applied Digital have all shed about that much if not more during the same period.Debt investors also appear spooked, and are demanding ever-higher returns from several firms in the sector.CoreWeave's CEO Mike Intrator has said that the market is acting "irrationally" and has expressed confidence in its business model. Some of the world's most consequential companies are queuing up for CoreWeave's infrastructure and other AI services.Several neocloud firms have their roots in the volatile crypto mining industry, made of companies that generate cryptocurrencies, like Bitcoin.Crypto miners use some of the same kind of physical infrastructure that is used to develop AI.CoreWeave was founded in 2017 with a focus on mining Ethereum.IREN, Core Scientific and Applied Digital also started in crypto mining.Their infrastructure left them well-positioned when AI exploded in 2022 with the introduction of OpenAI's ChatGPT.One outlier is Nebius, which was known as Yandex NV when it was part of Russia's version of Google before splitting off and changing its name in 2024.Now, the success of these firms hinges on the fate of major AI developers and hyperscalers – even larger data centre operators which neocloud firms often count as key customers."There is just an enormous amount of spending getting injected into the system," said Melissa Otto, head of Visible Alpha Research at S&P Global. "It's an arms race."And neoclouds have benefitted.But the trade-off of their model is "greater financial risk" in the face of change, said Forrester VP and principal analyst Charlie Dai.That includes any adjustments that their Big Tech customers might make to their spending plans.This past week, when Microsoft and Google forecast less AI spending than Wall Street analysts had projected, shares in several neocloud firms tumbled.Much is also riding on Anthropic and OpenAI, which are both expected to start selling shares to the public in the months ahead.If AI proves to be a bubble – and bursts – neocloud firms "are definitely going to face collateral damage," said Bradley Tusk of Tusk Ventures.The future of the neoclouds also depend on their ability to keep borrowing, which gets more expensive as interest rates rise.In a recent social media post, Elon Musk suggested this challenge could lead more than 200 neoclouds to "see guppy-level death and consolidation", with the smallest firms being the most vulnerable. "Some will make it through, but not many," he added.For now, analysts at Yorkville Ives said demand for computing power still exceeds supply, adding that neoclouds are filling an important gap that larger data centre companies cannot fill.But to some, the neocloud sector's recent wobbles are concerning.Microsoft recently cancelled a deal with a British neocloud outfit called Nscale amid power supply issues which could last through to 2030.Australia's Firmus just shelved plans to start selling shares to the public.These developments come amid a public backlash against data centres and questions about how much value AI can add to worker productivity."There's reason to worry," said Johnson.

schema.headline: Neoclouds: These firms you've never heard of are feeding fears the AI bubble could burst

title: Stranded in the Cook Islands: Why I can't get home to Sri Lanka
description: I've been stuck on a tiny Pacific island for years and can't get a transit visa to fly homeImage source, SuppliedByAyeshea PereraAsia Digital Editor a
body: I've been stuck on a tiny Pacific island for years and can't get a transit visa to fly homeImage source, SuppliedByAyeshea PereraAsia Digital Editor and Dinuk HewawitharanaBBC SinhalaWhen Ruchira Ranasingha left Sri Lanka almost a decade ago, she could never have imagined she would end up stranded on a tiny archipelago in the South Pacific.The 50-year-old has now been stuck in the Cook Islands for three years. She tells the BBC she is desperate to go back to Sri Lanka and has even offered to go "handcuffed, bound and gagged".Ranasingha had been hoping to settle in New Zealand.After seeking asylum there, she says she followed an immigration adviser's recommendation to temporarily exit the country to apply for a work visa. But once in the Cook Islands, her application was rejected. And by leaving New Zealand, she had breached the terms of her existing asylum-linked visa.Now New Zealand is refusing to issue her a transit visa that would allow her to fly home to Sri Lanka.Australia is refusing too. The only other international destinations she can fly to from the Cook Islands - Tahiti and Hawaii - require her to give biometric information in New Zealand before any visa can be processed.As a result, she has no feasible way of leaving."My son - my only child - is getting married in November and I really want to be there for his wedding. My mother is so worried about what has happened to me that she is constantly in and out of hospital," she says through tears."I will do anything they ask of me - I just want to go home."Ranasingha left Sri Lanka in 2018 after being forced to close her small T-shirt factory due to a loss of business. Struggling to repay loans, she moved to Hong Kong to work as a domestic caregiver looking after elderly people and children.Her brother tells BBC Sinhala she had come under immense financial pressure. Her husband was a drug addict who died about seven years ago, he adds.In December 2022, Ranasingha headed to New Zealand, where she says she lived with a cousin on a two-month visit visa. As it came close to expiring, she says an immigration interpreter helped her apply for asylum on the grounds she was facing threats from lenders in Sri Lanka.She was granted an asylum seeker "open work visa", enabling her to work for almost any employer for a year. She found a job at a restaurant, she says, which ultimately agreed to sponsor an employment visa, which she believed would give her longer-term stability.But as asylum seekers generally cannot apply for other visas while their applications are processed in New Zealand, it was declined.That's when she got in touch with Immigration & Secretarial Services, a firm she claims told her a fresh application for an employment visa could be made from overseas. Email correspondence the BBC has seen shows its manager, Sylviane Gallant, saying she would initiate the process as soon as Ranasingha had left the country.So she booked a short stay in the Cook Islands while the application was made.It turned out to be a disastrous decision.Image source, AFP via Getty ImagesImage caption, Cook Islands is known for its beaches and volcanic peaks - but Ruchira Ranasingha is an involuntary guestShe was again refused the employment visa. And by leaving New Zealand, she had violated the terms of her existing visa. New Zealand authorities made it clear they would not grant her any future visas.Gallant claimed to make various interventions on her behalf, including writing to politicians including Chris Penk, New Zealand's then-immigration minister. But ultimately, Ranasingha says Gallant admitted the situation was her fault and told her "there was nothing more she could do"."She told me I was better off going home. There was nothing holding me there so I agreed to go."But when she turned up at the airport with an Air New Zealand ticket to Sri Lanka in hand, she was told she couldn't board the flight without a New Zealand transit visa.Three applications for a New Zealand transit visa were rejected. Authorities said they weren't convinced she would leave New Zealand. Four applications for Australian transit visas were rejected too.In one of its rejections, New Zealand suggested she explore other routes. But both the US state of Hawaii and the French Polynesian island of Tahiti told her she would need to provide biometric information before any visa could be processed - and that could only be done in person in New Zealand.Her latest application to New Zealand, which included all the details of the alternative routes she'd been trying, as well as her son's upcoming wedding and mother's failing health, was also rejected."I have lost so much money on tickets. For almost four years I have been just applying for visa after visa with nothing working out," she says, breaking down.Image source, SuppliedOn a collection of islands known for their sweeping sandy beaches and rugged volcanic peaks, just four hours from Auckland, Ranasingha has been an involuntary guest.She's luckier than others in her position, she says, with her hotel letting her stay free of charge in its staff accommodation and friendly locals providing her with food and clothing.One of the hotel directors even gave her a sewing machine, she says, enabling her to make a small income."My mother always tells me I must have done something good, for me to be in a place like this where people have been so kind to me," she tells the BBC.But it does little to ease the sense of being trapped.Ranasingha says the stress is impacting her health. "I am scared something is going to happen to me," she says."I don't know what her solution is, to be honest," says Auckland-based immigration law specialist Alastair McClymont.She had received "terrible advice" which "certainly" could not have come from a genuine immigration lawyer, he says, pointing to an industry of "so-called immigration consultants" who charge people to lodge applications without fully understanding the risks involved. Ranasingha says she has parted with thousands of New Zealand dollars in fees to Immigration & Secretarial Services.The BBC reached out to Gallant but did not receive a response.McClymont suggests New Zealand authorities will not grant the transit visa because, as far as they are concerned, she has no intention of returning to Sri Lanka having made an asylum claim saying her life was in danger there.New Zealand co-ordinates with its neighbour Australia which means it won't want to let her transit either, he says, and France and the US are likely to reach similar conclusions.To leave, "she is going to have to transit through somewhere and no-one will want to take the risk."Immigration New Zealand told the BBC it had received multiple transit visa applications from Ranasingha - all declined "as we were not satisfied she has a genuine intention to transit through New Zealand".When asked why one couldn't be granted even when Ranasingha had offered to be handcuffed and escorted, a representative of the immigration minister's office said those measures do not prevent individuals from making an asylum claim.Australia's interior ministry said it would not comment on individual cases. It said any non-citizens travelling to Australia "must satisfy the requirements of the Migration Act 1958 (the Act) and the Migration Regulations 1994".Meanwhile, Ranasingha's family have been trying to see if the Sri Lankan government can help. Her brother says they have tried "every possible avenue... but so far we haven't been able to get anywhere on this".Sri Lanka's foreign ministry told the BBC it was "taking all necessary steps to facilitate her return to Sri Lanka from the Cook Islands. Officials of the Sri Lankan High Commission in Wellington, New Zealand, as well as the relevant New Zealand authorities, are working closely with the Ministry of Foreign Affairs on this matter."But Ranasingha's brother is deeply worried."Her mental state is not good," he tells BBC Sinhala."One of the times we spoke, she told me that if they were not willing to get her back home alive, they might at least repatriate her body."Additional reporting by Kethaki Masilamani and Julianna KhanIf you've been affected by issues involving suicide or feelings of despair, details of organisations offering advice and support for people in the UK are available from BBC Action Line. Help and support outside the UK can be found at Befrienders Worldwide, external.

schema.headline: Stranded in the Cook Islands: Why I can't get home to Sri Lanka

title: The fight to save Canadian town threatened by Trump's tariffs
description: Figure caption, "We're going to fight" - How a paper mill's uncertain future could devastate tiny Quebec townByJessica MurphyCanada digital editor and
body: Figure caption, "We're going to fight" - How a paper mill's uncertain future could devastate tiny Quebec townByJessica MurphyCanada digital editor and Nadine YousifSenior Canada reporterAs you cross the Ottawa river into Témiscaming, Quebec, the paper mill takes up much of the horizon.The town itself was built over a century ago, around the mill and the region's forests  filled with pine, birch, spruce and fir. Now, the main employer and economic anchor sits idle after trade talks broke down between Canada and the US and President Donald Trump imposed more tariffs on the country.Most of the mill‘s 360 employees are out of work, kept afloat for the moment with partial pay from government tariff-relief. For some, like Nadine Suley, the shuttering of the mill could mark not just a lost livelihood, but a lost way of life. She is not "a city girl", and is heading out moose hunting later to take advantage of the short season, like much of the town. She quips they'll all need the free meat provided by the animals this year. "It's not just a job. It's our home," Suley says, adding that the US tariffs on her town feel like "a personal attack". In early October, American owner RYAM went ahead with an "economic shutdown" of the mill for "an indefinite period". Property values in Témiscaming fell almost overnight, and "For Sale" signs dot the yards of modest middle-class homes that make up most of the town. There are fears that essential service people - from grocery store clerks to the doctors at the small local hospital - could also be on their way out."If the mill goes down, it'll turn into a ghost town," says Ronnie Raymond, who like many in the town comes from a family of mill workers. "There'll be nothing, nothing left. There's no work for anybody, really. It's scary."Image source, BBC/Jessica MurphyImage caption, The paper mill has served as the economic engine of Témiscaming for over a century.At a high level, Canada's economy has weathered the ongoing trade war with the US, its largest customer. The national unemployment rate has remained largely steady at around 6.5% since Trump's tariffs were first implemented. It's been coupled with tepid but consistent economic growth.But a closer look at the numbers shows pockets of deep pain in industries directly hit by US tariffs of up to 50%, like steel, aluminium, automobiles and - in the case of  Témiscaming - lumber, pulp and paper. It raises questions about whether the Carney government is doing enough to help those struggling while a trade deal remains elusive."If there was 10% of job loss in Toronto or Montreal or Quebec City or Vancouver, it'd be all over the news, and it'd be a lot of pressure on the governments to do something,” says Stéphane Lefebvre, an employee and union leader, whose father and grandfather also worked at the mill. That economic pain could have ripple effects on the entire forestry industry in the region, including saw mills and trucking. One local contractor told the BBC he has already had to lay off 13 people.The last time the town faced a threat this existential was in 1973, when the mill's then-American owner threatened to shut it down, prompting the local workers and managers to come together and purchase it.They turned it into Tembec, a Quebec-owned, international company with branches across North America and France. The workers now hope to do it again, mobilising a coalition of locals who want to buy the plant back from RYAM, which purchased it in 2017. "We're hoping that lightning will hit twice," Lefebvre says, speaking inside the town's union hall.But he contends that they cannot do so without significant help from Prime Minister Mark Carney and the Quebec government, either in the form of tariff relief or financial support. Suley notes that the prime minister has placed emphasis on "buy local" and supporting Canadian workers since he was elected. Backing the town's bid to buy back the mill, she says, would be a way for Carney to fulfil that pledge. In an email to the BBC, RYAM said it would not comment on a potential sale of the plant or any prospective buyers.Image source, BBC/Nadine YousifImage caption, Stéphane Lefebvre, his father and grandfather all worked at the paper mill in Témiscaming.Mayor Alain Gauthier doesn't blame RYAM for its decision. He calls US tariffs "a bomb to shut down our manufacturing in Canada". He wants Ottawa to retaliate with its own duties on the board products coming into Canada from the US, currently tariff-free.And he says that while politicians have said Canada is in an economic war with the US, "in reality we see absolutely no evidence of war measures being taken". "We feel we got into a war with kid's water guns to fight back." Some, like Lefebvre, feel that forestry has taken a back seat in the fight to save other tariffed industries like steel and autos.This month, Industry Minister Mélanie Joly threatened Stelco - one of Canada's largest steelmakers - with financial penalties or a forced asset sale should they go ahead with the planned layoffs of some 500 workers due to steel tariffs pressure. Stelco in Hamilton, near Toronto, is owned by US-based Cleveland-Cliffs, which committed to keeping jobs in Canada when it bought the firm in 2024. Last week, Carney and Ontario Premier Doug Ford announced nearly C$9bn ($6.4bn; £4.8bn) to help Ontario's steel and auto sector. The funds will be used to help the industries modernise, strengthen domestic demand and open new markets overseas, they said.Sébastien Lemire, the elected MP for Témiscaming from the Bloc Québécois party, told the BBC that he is "very concerned and worried" about what he calls inaction from the Carney government to support the town and Quebec's forestry industry more broadly.A spokesperson for Minister Joly told the BBC in a statement that the government has made available $400m to support the forestry sector in rural and remote areas.It has also launched a programme to help businesses impacted by tariffs to access cash-flow while they work to pivot away from US markets. On the Témiscaming mill, the spokesperson said that the government "is actively working with all parties involved to find a viable solution to the issues facing the company, while responsibly managing Canadians' dollars."Image source, Supplied/Stéphane LefebvreImage caption, Témiscaming residents gathered for a Union-led rally to support the mill's workers and draw attention to the woes of the lumber industry. In August, after the breakdown in trade talks, the US imposed 50% duties on a some C$28bn of Canadian goods, including wood and paper products like pulp, stationery and boxes. Canada in response imposed its own "dollar-for-dollar" counter-tariffs. The Témiscaming mill, which produces paperboard used in frozen-food packaging across North America and in the scratch-off lottery tickets commonly found at convenience stores, sends roughly 75% of its production to the US.Trump argues these import taxes boost US manufacturing and create jobs - essentially seeking to protect US workers who could face similar fates to those in Témiscaming. Frank Dottori has been through all of this before. Now in his 80s and retired in Témiscaming, he was an engineer at the mill that was instrumental in organising its employees in the 1970s to take a 10% cut in order to collectively purchase it. He went on to become CEO.Their ambitions were seen as foolish at the time, and he recalls being "politely ejected" by the Quebec premier when he first came knocking for support. But they prevailed with the help of the labour union and an ex-employee with executive experience and plenty of swagger. Dottori attributes their success to this person's forceful charisma.Dottori said the new generation of workers need someone just as bold."Does the local group have that? Highly unlikely. Can they get it? Yeah, if they organise themselves," he said. Image source, BBC/Nadine YousifImage caption, Frank Dottori led the effort to buy the Témiscaming mill in the 1970s during a period of economic hardship It is also imperative, he says, that US tariffs be lifted to restore the mill's long-term economic viability, at least in the short term.Many workers in Témiscaming say they are placing some hope in the upcoming US midterm elections to put pressure on Trump — whose approval ratings have fallen among Americans, according to polls — to ease some of his tariffs on Canada."We'll take any help we can get," Suley says, adding: "There are Americans that care what's going on, and it's affecting them too."There are signs the Trump administration is taking note of that pressure, with some tariffs on Canadian goods lifted last week after lobbying from Republican Maine Senator Susan Collins, who is running for re-election in November. Those changes don't apply to products made at Témiscaming's mill, however.Suley and others hope a resolution will come quickly, before winter, when sub-zero temperatures could freeze equipment at the idle plant, causing damage that would make reopening even more difficult.In the meantime, Lefebvre says he is committed to making the dream of local ownership of the mill a reality, regardless of what happens."We're in Game Seven right now," he says. "We're gonna play till the last whistle."

schema.headline: The fight to save Canadian town threatened by Trump's tariffs

title: More than 5,000 die from Ebola in DR Congo's deadliest outbreak
description: More than 5,000 people have died from an ongoing Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of Congo, government data shows. Eight of 26 provinces are
body: More than 5,000 people have died from an ongoing Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of Congo, government data shows. Eight of 26 provinces are now affected, with more than 10,300 confirmed cases.The outbreak, which started in May, became the country's deadliest in its history in August, public health officials said. The current case fatality rate is 48.6%.In its latest update, the health ministry said the epicentre of the epidemic remains in the Ituri province, in the north-east of the country, which is a conflict zone, making it harder to contain the virus.Cases have also been confirmed in Kenya, Nigeria and Uganda.This marks the 17th outbreak in DR Congo's history, according to the United Nations (UN), and the second largest in history.The World Health Organization (WHO) office in Africa said a "continued scale-up of key control measures, greater access to affected areas, and community outreach" is needed to end the outbreak. Testing and treatment are under way, along with clinical trials of vaccines, it added. The Bundibugyo species is behind the current outbreak, but there is not yet any treatment or vaccine for this strain. DR Congo's previous deadliest outbreak saw 2,299 deaths recorded between 2018-2020, the UN said. The deadliest in history occurred in West Africa between 2014 and 2016, killing more than 11,325 people and spread across several countries, including Italy, the UK and United States, according to the WHO.The UN warns that the current outbreak is "taking lives at a much faster rate". Ebola is a rare, deadly disease caused by a virus, and symptoms come on suddenly. As the disease progresses, vomiting and diarrhoea develop and it can lead to organ failure. Some, but not all, patients develop internal and external bleeding.The virus spreads from one person to another by contact with infected bodily fluids such as blood or vomit.Adding to the challenge of treating the disease, some health workers and a politician have been attacked while responding to the outbreak.Earlier this week, a nurse was killed and another health worker seriously injured in an attack when responding to an Ebola alert. Local youths had accused them of contaminating water sources and spreading the virus, according to the UN-backed Radio Okapi.Last month, a politician was beaten to death after promoting measures to stop the spread of Ebola, while in August, the Red Cross said its volunteers had been injured and an ambulance set on fire in 11 violent incidents in the outbreak's first 100 days.In Uganda, two people died and 20 cases were recorded shortly after the outbreak started, but no cases have been reported since August. Travel restrictions remain in place for those crossing into the country from neighbouring DR Congo.In Kenya, there have been nine confirmed cases and two recorded deaths.Two suspected cases were identified in Nigeria on Saturday, its disease control centre said, adding that the individuals have been isolated and they are undergoing testing. Earlier in October, one woman was confirmed to have the disease in the country but was flown to Switzerland for further treatment.The likelihood of infection for people in the Europe area is "very low," the European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control said.

schema.headline: More than 5,000 die from Ebola in DR Congo's deadliest outbreak

title: Global nature talks reach deal but money remains an issue
description: In Armenia's capital this week a fight between politicians broke out - not the mass brawl in its parliament that was so widely documented on social me
body: In Armenia's capital this week a fight between politicians broke out - not the mass brawl in its parliament that was so widely documented on social media - but between delegates from nearly 200 countries. The world's nations have been gathered in Yerevan for nearly two weeks  negotiating, and arguing, over a new agreement on nature.Early on Saturday morning, hours after talks were due to finish, they finally agreed the key parts of a new action plan. "And that's it. Perfect," said the meeting president, Hambardzum Matevosyan. Four years earlier the same countries had signed a landmark deal committing to "halt and reverse" the decline of nature. That global deal in 2022 - the Global Biodiversity Framework - contained 24 targets including putting 30% of the world's land and seas into protection by the end of the decade.They agreed that action was urgent. The world is currently in a sixth mass extinction event with species becoming extinct at 100 times the natural rate because of human activities, scientists say.But according to the UN this week,, external the world is on track to achieve just one of those two dozen targets. As part of this week's deal, countries acknowledged they were falling behind."While not particularly exciting or detailed, it's good news that countries could reach agreement," said Catherine Weller, from environmental charity Fauna & Flora."We cannot just plod on to 2030 without a course correction; nature is critical to all life on Earth: to our economies, to our wellbeing," she added. This was echoed by Craig Bennett, CEO of The Wildlife Trusts, who told BBC News: "We are still seeing an appalling loss, threatening the collapse of ecosystems globally. We run out of words really about how serious this is."But he added "the better news is there are so many examples worldwide about how... to turn things around".Countries have put 623 million acres (252m hectares) of degraded land into protection, external - an area bigger than Greenland. Just last month the WWF praised conservation efforts which had achieved the recovery of key species including elephants, green sea turtles and tigers.Bluefin tuna comeback shows nature can recover, says WWFCountries have recognised the main barrier to accelerating those efforts is money. In 2022, they agreed they would put $30bn (£22.4bn) towards nature recovery efforts by the end of the decade, and mobilise a further $170bn from private sources.But years later many nations have been redirecting international aid to defence budgets and to deal with repeated energy shocks, such that pledges are not at the rate required to reach those targets, according to the UN. , externalAt this meeting, more than $1bn was pledged, with half of that coming from philanthropists including Leonardo DiCaprio's Re:wild organisation. Anna Ducros, a researcher at the International Institute for Environment and Development, said there had been some progress on countries committing to reducing subsidies for industries harmful to the environment."A concrete example is that governments subsidise large-scale fishing that is especially harmful for nature - for example, trawling."Ducros, who was in attendance at the talks, added: "Right now, we have the situation where governments are paying twice. "So they know that they need to increase spending on nature and climate, but at the same time, they're damaging nature."A specific funding pot, the Cali Fund, was previously set up for private companies that profit from using genetic material found in the environment to donate to. It was estimated up to $3.6bn could be raised annually -  at the start of the meeting just $10,000 had been pledged.Little progress was made on that issue - its voluntary nature makes it difficult to put pressure on companies, Bennett acknowledged."When you have countries that have rich biodiversity in them and you have companies trying to make money out of the genetic material found in those countries they should be paying those communities," he said. "That should not be controversial."One of the easier issues on the agenda was meant to be the approval of scientific reports into the state of nature. But a small group of countries, including Saudi Arabia and Russia, were reported to have frustrated that process."The attacks on science have bothered me a lot," French Ecological Transition Minister Monique Barbut was reported as saying by the AFP news agency. Next month countries will gather for the annual climate conference - COP31. Its own science body, the IPCC, has faced similar challenges in the past month with passing its own scientific reports and securing funding."This is such a blatant political move...and the IPCC is no such place for such political manoeuvring since the outputs are in humanity's interest," said Prof David Lee, from Manchester University, who has worked on previous reports.

schema.headline: Global nature talks reach deal but money remains an issue

title: Rahul Gandhi: India's opposition rallies against voter roll revision exercise
description: Tens of thousands gathered in Delhi for a rally demanding the resignation of India's chief election commissioner over a controversial revision of vote
body: Tens of thousands gathered in Delhi for a rally demanding the resignation of India's chief election commissioner over a controversial revision of voter lists.Organised by the opposition INDIA bloc and led by Rahul Gandhi's Congress party, the protest drew many of the alliance's most prominent leaders in a show of strength against Prime Minister Narendra Modi's government.Protesters waved flags and chanted "Save the vote, save the country" and "Vote thief, give up power".It was the latest in a series of protests over electoral roll revision that the opposition says has removed eligible voters to benefit the Bharatiya Janata Party. The BJP and the Election Commission deny the allegations.The crowds gathered at Ramlila Maidan, a sprawling ground in central Delhi known for hosting major political and cultural events. Some protesters sang and danced to patriotic Bollywood songs, while others waited beneath a large canopy in the colours of the Indian flag to hear opposition leaders speak.Gandhi and several senior opposition leaders arrived at the venue in an open jeep, travelling through crowds of cheering supporters.The event was also attended by Congress leaders Sonia Gandhi and Mallikarjun Kharge, alongside leaders of regional parties such as Mamata Banerjee, Akhilesh Yadav, Mehbooba Mufti, Supriya Sule and Tejashwi Yadav.Addressing the crowds, Rahul Gandhi said those gathered had sent a message to Modi, Home Minister Amit Shah and Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar."This is not the voice of a single political party or of politicians. It is the voice of India's youth, women, farmers and workers," he said."We will not allow democracy to be destroyed in India. We will not allow the constitution to be destroyed."Other opposition leaders echoed Gandhi's criticism of the Election Commission. Congress president Kharge said the alliance would continue its campaign until Kumar resigned, while Banerjee pledged to keep fighting against what she described as threats to democracy.Speaking to reporters in Delhi on Sunday, senior BJP leader and federal minister JP Nadda accused the opposition of trying to create unrest and destabilise the government under the guise of defending democracy.He described the rally as a "calculated conspiracy to plunge the nation into anarchy - in the name of democracy".At the centre of the dispute is an exercise known as the Special Intensive Revision (SIR), which has resulted in more than 130 million names being removed from India's draft electoral rolls.The Election Commission says the exercise is intended to remove duplicate registrations and the names of people who have died, moved away or are otherwise ineligible to vote. It says eligible voters who have been wrongly excluded can seek to have their names restored.But opposition parties allege that the process is removing legitimate voters and could benefit the governing BJP in future elections.The controversy deepened in September when The Indian Express newspaper reported, external that Kumar had made key decisions about the revision despite repeated objections from the two other election commissioners.The poll panel said differences of opinion were normal in any institution and did not affect its functioning.Sunday's rally followed weeks of protests over the voter-list revision, including demonstrations by student groups and the Gen Z-led Cockroach Janta Party (CJP). Last month, Gandhi led tens of thousands on a march from central Delhi's Connaught Place to the Supreme Court, demanding Kumar's resignation.The CJP also backed Sunday's rally but chose not to participate. Its founder Abhijeet Dipke said the group wanted to maintain its independence from established political parties.The event took place under strict conditions imposed by Delhi Police. According to local media reports, organisers were required to end the gathering by 5pm, install CCTV cameras at the venue and ensure that protesters did not march beyond the designated grounds.The restrictions came against a backdrop of tensions over the policing of demonstrations in the capital. On 10 October, several leaders of the CJP were detained during protests against Kumar, while BBC reporters witnessed police dragging demonstrators away and beating some with batons.At Ramlila Maidan, however, the atmosphere was largely peaceful, with people of different ages and professions turning out to express their concerns about the integrity of India's elections."We don't even know if this is a people's mandate or a stolen mandate," Isha, a development sector professional from Delhi, told the BBC.Deepro Guha, a lawyer from Delhi, said he was concerned about the way the revision had been carried out."It's important because voting is the basis of democracy. If people's names are removed without any explanation, there is a problem," he said.

schema.headline: Rahul Gandhi: India's opposition rallies against voter roll revision exercise

title: Crypto firm Binance covers 90% of losses after $6.3bn hack
description: Binance, the world's largest cryptocurrency exchange, says it has covered 90% of the $6.3bn (£4.7bn) assets stolen in a hack on Thursday.The remaining
body: Binance, the world's largest cryptocurrency exchange, says it has covered 90% of the $6.3bn (£4.7bn) assets stolen in a hack on Thursday.The remaining 10% may take longer to source in the required amounts, the company added. Binance has consistently pledged to cover 100% of the losses from what is suspected to be crypto's biggest hack on record and said it has set aside more than $6.34bn in company funds to do so."Binance will absorb the financial impact of these stolen funds, not our users," the company said in a statement on Saturday.In an update on Sunday, Binance said withdrawals had been restored on several of its networks, after they were suspended following the hack.It previously said withdrawals would be resumed in phases.The Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) said on Saturday that North Korea was responsible for the attack.The FBI said it had observed hackers converting stolen assets into a type of cryptocurrency called Ethereum and that it is expected that the assets will then be converted again using decentralised finance and instant swap services.Two analytics firms previously told the BBC they had robust intelligence pointing to North Korean state-backed hacking unit the Lazarus Group, also known as TraderTraitor - which was specifically named by the FBI - as the likely culprits.Speaking to reporters on Saturday night, US President Donald Trump said, external the US is still unsure who the culprits are."We're learning about it. We don't know if it's North Korea - but if it is, we'll talk to North Korea about it," he said.Binance said it had replenished the stolen assets using various funds and its own corporate treasury.All holdings of the cryptocurrencies bitcoin, Ethereum and Tether are covered, along with seven other widely-traded crypto assets, the company said.From Bitcoin to Binance: Crypto terms and what they meanThe hack is believed to be the largest in history, eclipsing the record of a $1.5bn heist on the Bybit exchange in 2025 - for which the FBI also said North Korea was responsible.North Korea has always denied involvement in these attacks.Binance's initial investigation suggested an engineer's laptop was compromised, which allowed access to unauthorised withdrawals, but a later update said they had uncovered "additional points of breach". Richard Teng, Binance's co-chief executive officer, said the hack was carried out by more than one person, and the hackers used sophisticated methods to hide their tracks, such as a "self-destruct mechanism".On Friday, the company said it had frozen around $3bn of stolen assets after working with law enforcement, intelligence firms and partners. The investigation is ongoing, it added. The US Secret Service said on Friday it is "working around the clock" with private sector partners "to identify, freeze, trace, and recover funds" stolen from Binance.Binance, founded in China in 2017, lets users buy, sell and trade digital assets - it is estimated to have hundreds of millions of users worldwide.Crypto is a digital asset, which doesn't exist physically and is instead accessed via digital wallets or computers.

schema.headline: Crypto firm Binance covers 90% of losses after $6.3bn hack

title: Alaska Senate candidate denies knowing about alleged plot to put 2 Dan Sullivans on ballot
description: Democratic Senate candidate Mary Peltola has denied she knew anything about an alleged "scheme" that led to two men named Dan Sullivan standing in the
body: Democratic Senate candidate Mary Peltola has denied she knew anything about an alleged "scheme" that led to two men named Dan Sullivan standing in the Alaska Senate race.The denial comes as the Trump administration continues to escalate a criminal investigation into the matter, including a request for election officials to separate ballots that rank retired teacher Dan J Sullivan.Senator Dan S Sullivan, the incumbent Republican running for re-election, and allies have accused the Democrats of trying to confuse voters. The Alaska race is considered by analysts to be one of the tightest in the upcoming US midterm elections, which will decide which party controls Congress."I just want to clear the air," Peltola said while speaking to voters on Thursday. "I knew nothing about any other candidate on the ballot except for me and the incumbent. That is all I have ever known about. I am not interested in tricking voters."Alaska's Republican Governor Mike Dunleavy ordered an official inquiry earlier this week into the alleged scheme. Heyman did not immediately provide details of specific crimes his office would investigate.Both Dan Sullivans have been running for the open Senate seat for some time. Still, controversy erupted earlier this week when The New York Times, external reported that Peltola's team worked with people who tried to recruit spoiler candidates in the Senate race.The Times's report alleged that people connected to Peltola's campaign, as well as senior aides at the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee (DSCC), worked to try to recruit Dan J Sullivan, a retired teacher who lives in a remote fishing village, to stand in the Senate race.The paper said it had seen text messages and interviewed 12 people who participated in or were told of the plan, or were would-be candidates who the team also tried to recruit. The BBC has not independently verified the reporting.The Peltola campaign has denied those reports and Sullivan has denied any links to her campaign.But those denials have not stopped the justice department (DOJ) and Republicans from attacking Peltola. The DOJ has begun issuing subpoenas targeting Democratic officials allegedly connected to the recruitment effort, according to CBS News, the BBC's US news partner. No charges had been filed as of Friday evening. "There is both a civil investigation and a criminal investigation that are ongoing," Michael Heyman, the US attorney for the district of Alaska, said at a Friday afternoon press conference. Later that day, lawyers for the Trump administration asked a federal judge to issue an order before Monday that would direct state election officials "to preserve and segregate" all ballots that rank Dan J Sullivan.Alaska's ranked-choice voting system means that voters could select both Sullivans if they are unsure at the ballot box.Associate Attorney General Stanley Woodward argued in court documents that the move would be to investigate whether such ranking "was the product of voter confusion, should such an investigation become necessary"."These modest precautionary measures will be impossible after Election Day, so there is good cause for expedited consideration," he said. But the state's Republican attorney general - the top prosecutor in the state - asked the court to toss the lawsuit and said the request from the Trump administration was "inappropriate and not even possible given Alaskan voters' vital right to ballot secrecy".The filing said there was "no reason for this Court to entertain this meritless lawsuit any longer". Scott Kendall, an attorney who worked with Republican Senator Lisa Murkowski in her 2010 and 2016 campaigns, told the BBC he was sceptical the actions described in the New York Times story broke the law.Alaska law does not have specific good-faith requirements for candidates, Kendall explained - noting that spoiler candidates sometimes emerged in their contests. "I freely admit there could be more facts, but I'm not going to speculate they exist," he said.The spectre of a federal crimes could come into play if there was potential evidence of campaign finance violations, Kendall, as well as other legal experts, told the BBC. But such evidence has not yet emerged.Kendall believed the primary risk to Peltola from the allegations is "absolute reputational harm". The Trump administration filed a federal lawsuit last week aimed at preventing the certification of the result if the Trump-backed Sullivan loses, arguing the presence of both of them on the ballot could confuse voters.On Wednesday, the justice department amended its lawsuit to include the reporting by the Times, citing significant sections of the story as well as Governor Mike Dunleavy's announcement of an investigation.A federal judge has expedited consideration and will weigh motions to dismiss brought by Alaska election officials and backed by the Peltola campaign and voting rights groups.The legal action comes days before voters across the US head to the polls. This race in Alaska is among the closest-watched in the country, as it could be the deciding factor in who controls the Senate. The non-partisan Cook Political Report currently classifies the race as a toss-up. As the final weekend of campaigning approaches, President Donald Trump will appear at back-to-back rallies in Kansas and Iowa on Sunday.The in-person appearances were previously cancelled, but a source familiar with planning told the BBC that they were rescheduled to accommodate remote appearances by Trump at tele-rallies.

schema.headline: Alaska Senate candidate denies knowing about alleged plot to put 2 Dan Sullivans on ballot

title: G20 'family photo' cancelled after protests over presence of Russian minister
description: European diplomats have refused to stand for an official photo with Russia's Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov at the G20 Foreign Ministers' Meeting, lea
body: European diplomats have refused to stand for an official photo with Russia's Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov at the G20 Foreign Ministers' Meeting, leading to the American hosts cancelling the planned picture.Two officials confirmed to BBC the cancellation of the "family photo" scheduled for Friday, which usually include representatives from all nations attending."Let me say this directly to the Russian Foreign Minister: We all know who the aggressor in this war is," UK Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband later told his Russian counterpart at the summit, accusing his government of killing innocent civilians in Ukraine.The meeting is being hosted in Atlanta by US Secretary of State Marco Rubio. Speaking with G20 foreign ministers on Friday, Miliband said that member countries  must "work harder to secure just and lasting peace in Ukraine". "Russia's war continues to cause colossal global harm - including the deaths of thousands of innocent civilians and disruption that hits energy and supplies and worsens food insecurity," he said. "This war is not simply a test for Europe or for Nato - it requires all of us to apply economic and diplomatic pressure to deprive Putin of the revenues that perpetuate this barbaric war."Ukraine is not a G20 member but has been invited to similar meetings in recent years. However, Ukraine was not invited to this meeting.One British official told the BBC: "The UK has a longstanding policy not to have direct, bilateral engagement with Russian ministers since the invasion of Ukraine and we are not about to change that".Relations between Ukraine and the US have been particularly tense this month, with a diplomatic standoff between Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky and US President Donald Trump over Kyiv's strikes on oil infrastructure within Russia.A US official said the photo was cancelled "after it became clear some of the delegations were unwilling to participate in a joint photo"."Rather than allow a ceremonial photo opportunity to become a diplomatic distraction, the US decided to forgo the photo and keep the focus on the substantive discussions," the official said.In contrast to Ukraine, relations between the US and Russia appear to have partially thawed in recent weeks, as Trump waived some sanctions and agreed a deal to import Russian diesel for the American market. The move comes as Trump attempts to lower fuel prices in the US ahead of midterm elections on Tuesday, after months spent grappling with the political consequences of the Iran war.Ukraine and its European allies have heavily criticised Trump's deal with Russian President Vladimir Putin.Zelensky called it "a gift" to Putin that amounts to "an investment in a war that must be ended, not prolonged".Trump said his decision to suspend several Russian sanctions is an effort to keep Moscow at the negotiating table in the war between Russia and Ukraine.Putin has said Russia, which introduced a ban on diesel exports earlier this year, is willing to supply both the US and global markets with oil and petroleum products.Still, the US State Department this week said it had approved the sale of more than $2bn worth of Patriot missiles to Ukraine, a critically needed munition for the country's air defences to protect itself from Russian attacks.  Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022 and currently controls approximately a fifth of Ukrainian territory.Moscow has in recent weeks intensified its deadly missile and drone attacks on Kyiv and other Ukrainian cities.

schema.headline: G20 'family photo' cancelled after protests over presence of Russian minister

title: Shops looted as German cost-of-living protests turn violent
description: Figure caption, Watch: Protesters clash with police and shops looted in GermanyByJames ChaterUpdated 5 hours agoRioters looted shops in central Frankf
body: Figure caption, Watch: Protesters clash with police and shops looted in GermanyByJames ChaterUpdated 5 hours agoRioters looted shops in central Frankfurt late on Saturday as clashes erupted in German cities over the cost of living.Besides Frankfurt - Germany's financial hub - there were incidents of violence in Berlin, Cologne and Hamburg, with police saying they used water cannon to disperse protesters who were targeting emergency workers with fireworks, stones and bottles.Thousands joined largely peaceful demonstrations earlier in the day. They were organised by the campaign group Gen Z regelt - meaning "Gen Z takes charge" - to protest against underfunding in schools, the high cost of living, public spending cuts and military service.The unrest in Germany follows similar youth-led mass protests in France, where more than 320,000 people also demonstrated on Saturday.On Sunday, Germany's Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt told Bild newspaper that overnight police had prevented "violence like that seen in Paris" in recent weeks and called for "harsh punishments" for rioters and looters.Overnight, a large section of Frankfurt's main shopping street was closed off by police. A police spokesperson said many arrests were made in the city.Authorities in Frankfurt, Munich and Berlin reported as many as 18,000 protesters, roughly half of what the organisers had estimated on their website. German media say tens of thousands protested in German cities on Saturday.Gen Z regelt spokesperson Lina Friedrich said the demonstrations were "to fight for peace and freedom, rather than for war and coercion".She said: "What matters most to us is better support for the health and education systems. We are against compulsory military service and we are in favour of a fairer distribution of the burden."Image source, ReutersImage caption, Police detain a demonstrator dressed as Batman in FrankfurtOn Saturday night Frankfurt police said "violent riots" were occurring in the city centre and that special police units had been deployed.The windows of several shops had been smashed and molotov cocktails were thrown at emergency services, police said.Officials said the windows of a gun shop were smashed and that they had seized two weapons after arresting a suspect. People also broke into other shops, stealing items like trainers.Roman Poseck, interior minister of Hesse state, of which Frankfurt is the biggest city, said that "around 100 clearly identified left-wing extremists" had infiltrated the protest in the city. He added that it was "shameful" how the protests had ended."We all have those images from France in our minds - looting, burning houses, burning police vehicles, and attacks on police officers... France must not be held up as a model in this regard."Police said the situation calmed down overnight into Sunday in the city.Image source, ReutersImage caption, People try to break through a window of a Frankfurt shop selling weaponsSimilar instances took place in other German cities, following largely peaceful demonstrations. In Cologne, police said officers were attacked near the main train station, with bottles thrown and a bicycle launched.Cologne's police chief Johannes Hermanns said it was "deeply saddening that young people who wanted to peacefully demonstrate for their future were infiltrated today by extremists who had nothing but violence in mind". A smaller demonstration in the evening in Berlin - following larger protests in the day - resulted in 27 police officers being injured, and up to 56 people temporarily detained, Berlin police said.In Hamburg, people dressed in black set off fireworks and set barricades on fire, with public broadcaster NDR reporting that 120 people were arrested.The protests in Germany took place on the same day as other large-scale demonstrations in Europe. In France, more than 320,000 people took part in a third consecutive weekend of largely peaceful protests in cities across the country, demanding action on the high cost of living and poor public services, especially in the education sector.Thousands of police officers were deployed across the country, and officers fired tear gas at demonstrators in some cities.There were more than 770 arrests across France during the demonstrations on Saturday, roughly half as many as the previous week's protests, the French interior ministry said.Figure caption, Thousands demonstrate in Paris as protests spread across EuropeFrench Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez said a police officer had been injured by a molotov cocktail and French prosecutors later launched an attempted murder probe.Police in Paris said several hundred rioters had attacked security forces with projectiles.French protest organisers, the Gilet Jaune, or Yellow Vests, have said dozens of protesters have been seriously injured during recent demonstrations across the country, with many hurt by "grenades".France suspended the use of one type of stun grenade while policing student protests in early October after a 15-year-old's hand was blown off, but French newspaper Le Monde has reported, external that police have continued to use a different model in subsequent protests.Protests also took place in Italy, with some clashes between police and demonstrators in Rome and Turin.In Portugal, police moved to clear a new tent camp that had been assembled after thousands marched to protest against a rental bill that they argue could worsen a housing crisis in the country, where house prices have more than doubled over the past decade.Mostly young protesters have recently taken to the streets in a swathe of European nations: France, Belgium, Ireland, Spain, Portugal, Italy, Greece, Serbia and Albania.While the specific demands vary from country to country, the protesters have largely focused on cost-of-living issues, such as access to housing, the quality of education and cuts to public services.

schema.headline: Shops looted as German cost-of-living protests turn violent

title: Democrats are used to heartbreak in Texas - will Talarico turn the tide?
description: Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Democrats hope James Talarico, 37, could end a decades-long winning streak for Republicans in Texas Senate ra
body: Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Democrats hope James Talarico, 37, could end a decades-long winning streak for Republicans in Texas Senate racesByNorth America correspondent in Lubbock, TexasThe race for a US Senate seat in Texas may prove crucial in determining which party controls Congress next year – a significant prize in its own right - but for both parties it represents so much more than that.For the Democrats, their losing streak in statewide elections now stretches back more than three decades. In the second most populous state in America, liberals have been in the wilderness for a generation.But polls suggest their candidate, 37-year-old James Talarico, may be on the verge of breaking through and turning a Texas Senate seat blue for the first time since 1988. That would be a dream scenario for Democrats - and a potential nightmare for Republicans."If the Democrats do pull it off, I think it's going to cause a lot of soul searching and a lot of psychological damage to the Republican Party in Texas and nationwide," said Brendan Steinhauser, a Texas-based Republican campaign strategist.These dramatic stakes help explain how this Senate race has rocketed to become the most expensive in US history, with total spending reaching more than half a billion dollars.For Talarico, it has been a remarkable rise for a candidate who in 2025 was a relatively unknown state-level Democrat. At the Fiesta Center in Lubbock, Texas, on Tuesday night, the line to see the softly spoken former teacher, who studied to be a Christian minister, stretched around the building and down the wide parking lot to a busy road.In this dusty western plains town of about 250,000, which voted overwhelmingly for President Donald Trump two years ago, a visit from a major Democratic candidate on the eve of an election was unusual."It's just so amazing to watch," said Aaron Gonzalez, the Democratic Party chair for Hockley County, which borders Lubbock. "This time is different."Image source, ReutersWhen Talarico took the stage before an estimated 3,000 supporters – with another thousand listening on speakers outside - his pitch was a familiar one for many national Democrats this year, albeit with a Texas twist.He railed against a conservative political establishment that he said is insensitive to the economic hardship of average Americans. He condemned the corrosive influence of big money in politics. And he promised to advance a "comprehensive anti-corruption agenda" in the Senate."Texans are ready for change," he said. "We are done with the extremism and the corruption. We're done with the politics of division, and we are ready for something new."The slogan for his final two weeks of campaigning – "clear eyes, full hearts, can't lose" – is taken from Friday Night Lights, a popular early 2000s TV show about a plucky small-town Texas high school football team.His music playlist leans heavily on twangy Texas country music.  He celebrates Texas breakfast tacos, quotes legendary Texas singer-songwriter Lyle Lovett and frequently mentions that his ties to the state go back eight generations.In the Lubbock audience, Andrew Robinson, a student from nearby Texas Tech University, liked what he heard. But the 26-year-old's optimism was tempered by an entire lifetime spent watching Democrats try, and fail, to get a toehold in the state."A Talarico win would mean so much," he said. "I haven't been keen on wanting to stay in Texas. And if the government were to change, it could give me a reason."Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Donald Trump won Texas in the 2016, 2020 and 2024 presidential electionsFor Republicans, a Democratic win in Texas would have a very different meaning.At roughly the same time Talarico was addressing his supporters in the Fiesta Center, Trump – alongside the Republican Party's Senate candidate Ken Paxton – was just a few miles away, in a venue twice the size."If you go out and vote, we're going to have a tremendous win in Texas," the president told the crowd.Trump's visit to reliably-Republican Lubbock suggests the party is concerned about turnout even in the most conservative portions of the state. It is a worry that has been echoed by other Texas Republicans."Understand, we could lose Texas," Texas Senator Ted Cruz said in his podcast on Friday. "The Democrats are massively out-turning-out the Republicans."Don Huffines, who is running for election as the state's chief financial officer, issued an even more dire warning. "Texas is the foundation of the Republican Party in America," he posted on X. "When the foundation breaks, it all falls apart. When we lose Texas, we lose the USA."For weeks now, party leaders have been warning that a liberal breakthrough in the Lone Star State could have dire consequences.They fear a Talarico win would motivate more local Democrats to run for statewide and federal offices. Better quality candidates with more funding could lead to a snowball effect similar to the Democratic inroads seen in other southern states, such as Georgia, North Carolina and Virginia."I think that it's pretty clear that Republicans, especially candidates, consultants, operatives, and others who are active in the party, see that this is a real threat," said Steinhauser. "The days of waving this off and saying that Texas would never turn blue are over."Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Republican candidate Ken Paxton has a Trump endorsement - and some past controversies in Texas politicsFor the Texas Senate race to come to the point where recent polls suggest Talarico has a slim but stable lead has required a unique confluence of events and political dynamics – a "perfect storm", in the words of Steinhauser."Everything that could go well for the Democrats is going well," he said, "and everything that could go badly for the Republicans is going badly."But it is also a whirlwind that, in a significant part, has been sown over the past year by Trump himself.The national environment for Republicans is a harsh one. Voters are frustrated with high consumer costs, including the price of petrol, and largely blame Trump's tariff policies and the Iran war. Political corruption has become an issue of growing concern. Democrats, independents and many Republicans in a recent Cook political report poll identified "greedy billionaires and corporations" and politicians seeking "personal gain" as the ones to blame.Figure caption, What's at stake for Trump in the US midterms?Texas-specific issues have also contributed to a hostile climate for the in-power party.Polling and recent special elections in Texas indicate that Hispanic voters – many of whom switched to Trump to help him win the White House in 2024 – have soured on the administration's immigration enforcement policies. Hispanics make up nearly a third of the state's population - and in more than a week of early voting in Texas, they have been casting ballots in historically large numbers.Data centre construction, which Texas Republicans had touted as a welcome investment in the state, has drawn widespread criticism, particularly in rural areas that have traditionally been solidly conservative.Texas Governor Greg Abbott, in his own tight re-election race, recently announced a one-year moratorium on AI construction in the state – a reflection of how quickly the issue has become a political liability."It's bad for Republicans," one Texas political strategist, who asked to remain anonymous, told the BBC. "We're asking a whole lot of the electorate at this point for us to continue to be the guys in charge."Figure caption, Watch: Texas voters share concerns over cost of living ahead of midtermsThen there's the baggage that Paxton, who defeated longtime incumbent Senator John Cornyn in a contentious primary campaign earlier this year, brings to the race.The 63-year-old Republican successfully painted the 74-year-old Cornyn as too old and too out-of-touch with Texas conservatives. He received a late boost, just days before his run-off election victory over Cornyn, in the form of a Trump endorsement."Ken Paxton has gone through a lot, in many cases, very unfairly, but he is a Fighter, and knows how to WIN," Trump wrote on Truth Social. "Our Country needs Fighters, and also Loyalty to the Cause of Greatness."The "a lot" the president referenced Paxton going through includes a 2015 federal indictment on charges of securities fraud – later dropped – and a 2023 impeachment by the Republican-controlled Texas House of Representatives on corruption, bribery and abuse of power charges. The Texas Senate would later acquit Paxton after Trump intervened to pressure state Republican leaders.All of this has meant that Paxton has more than a few critics – and enemies - in Texas, including within his own party.GUIDE: What are the US midterms?EXPLAINED: Why Trump's approval rating matters in the midtermsIN DEPTH: The Republicans walking a Trump tightropeTalarico, by contrast, has proven to be an effective candidate. The state legislator defeated a well-known opponent, Dallas Congresswoman Jasmine Crockett, in the Democratic primary.Since earning the nomination, he has maintained his polling lead despite a withering onslaught of negative advertising - much of it funded by the world's richest man Elon Musk, whose SpaceX company is based in Texas. Musk alone has funnelled more than $170m into the race. Trump's MAGA Inc. committee has chipped in $40m.While Paxton has proven to be an ineffective fundraiser, the third-party money spent on his behalf has blanketed the airwaves in the state – spilling over into sporting events involving Texas teams that air across the nation.They have targeted Talarico for his past comments supporting transgender people, for calling "radicalised white men" a domestic terrorism threat and for criticising the fossil fuel and beef industries – two powerful interests in the state.Talarico has distanced himself from some of those earlier comments, arguing many were taken out of context and "missed the mark" or were "deliberately provocative" or "cringy".Meanwhile, the Texas Democrat has proven to be a historically successful fundraiser, amassing more than $140m in donations over the course of his campaign and setting a three-month fundraising record for a Senate candidate.The funding has allowed Talarico to hit back at Paxton, highlighting his past controversies, and defending himself from Republican attacks.He frequently leans into his religious upbringing – as the grandson of a Southern Baptist preacher who spent time in a seminary – leavening his stump speeches with biblical references.There is one particular passage Talarico has been partial to of late – the familiar Old Testament showdown between scrappy David and the giant Goliath."We are going up against our own Goliaths," he said in Lubbock. "The billionaire mega-donors, the corporate special interests, the entire Washington DC establishment. Their power is real, but so is ours."But the power of Texas Democrats has been overestimated in the past. In 2018, Congressman Beto O'Rourke posted his own historic fundraising numbers, generated serious national attention and ultimately lost to Texas Senator Cruz by just over 2%.Talarico's polling lead, while stable, continues to rest near the margin of error in most surveys. And last-minute Republican appeals, as well as Trump's repeated campaign visits, could spur conservatives to turn out in greater numbers on election day, erasing any Democratic early voting advantages.Inside the tiny Democratic Party office at a Talarico rally in Amarillo on Tuesday, retired schoolteacher Terri Mills listened to the candidate's stump speech.Despite acknowledging the decades of Democratic futility and false dawns, she said she was allowing herself to hope for a Democratic victory once again."I have gotten my hopes up before, you know," she said. "But I do feel that this time is a little different."Follow the twists and turns of Trump's second term with North America correspondent Anthony Zurcher's US Politics Unspun newsletter. schema.headline: Democrats are used to heartbreak in Texas - will Talarico turn the tide?
